newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: A cornered Pyongyang could strike out, warns U.S.
newsitem.headline: A cornered Pyongyang could strike out, warns U.S.

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific on Wednesday warned that forcing famine-hit North Korea into a corner could drive it to attack its southern neighbour, resulting in heavy loss of life.
Admiral Joseph Prueher said the severity of the famine in the North remained unclear, but Washington's immediate concern was that Pyongyang "retains a considerable military capability to lash out".

"Should they try and conduct a full-scale assault they will not prevail, but it would nonetheless be a very difficult situation with a lot of loss of life because of the military capability North Korea maintains," he said.
Prueher, commander-in-chief of U.S. forces in the Pacific, spoke at a meeting in Manila of the Pacific Basin Economic Council, which comprises more than 1,200 corporate members from 20 economies.

He said the United Nations, the United States and South Korea must remain vigilant against the threat of a North Korean military strike, "yet not squeeze or corner North Korea to the extent that they feel compelled to lash out".
The two Koreas remain technically at war since their 1950-53 Korean conflict ended only in a truce.
Separately, Prueher said the United States did not see China as a threat to U.S. interests at present.
The U.S. estimates that it will take China about 15 years before it could develop the full capability to project its forces beyond its borders, he said.

Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa, in a clear reference to China, urged nations with rival claims to the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea to respect international and bilateral agreements to ensure peace in the area.
"The Philippines stands firm on its commitment to...exert its utmost to prevent the eruption of an armed conflict in the area," he told the council.

Manila recently protested to Beijing against what it considered the incursion last month of Chinese naval ships in an area of the Spratlys that the Philippines claims. China says the ships were research vessels on a scientific mission.
Beijing insists all the islands in the South China Sea historically belongs to China. The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
